questions.q: How do you say "I like coffee" in French?
questions.why: French keeps an article where English drops one, and a general preference takes the definite article. Aimer, adorer, détester and préférer always take le, la or les, because you like the category and not a portion.

questions.q: What does à + les contract to?
questions.why: à contracts with le and les only: au, aux. de does the same: du, des. à la, à l', de la and de l' are left alone.

questions.q: « Je mange un poulet. » What does it actually mean?
choices: I'm eating at a chicken place
questions.why: The article decides how much: du poulet is an amount off a plate, un poulet is one entire bird, le poulet is chicken as a category. All three are grammatical; they describe different meals.

questions.q: Make it negative: « J'aime le fromage. »
questions.why: The collapse to de hits un, une, du, de la and des only. The definite article never changes after a negative.

questions.q: Make it negative: « C'est un livre. »
questions.why: After être the article survives untouched. That is the second exception to the negative rule, alongside the definite article.
à + le contracts to au. Writing à le is never possible.
de + le contracts to du. The same du also spells the partitive, so context tells you which one you are looking at: here it means "of the".
Eau is feminine, so the partitive would be de la, but the vowel forces de l'. Same for de l'argent and de l'huile.
After a negative verb, un, une, du, de la and des all collapse to de. J'ai une voiture becomes je n'ai pas de voiture.

questions.q: Il y a beaucoup ___ gens ici.
questions.why: Every expression of quantity is followed by bare de, even before a plural noun: beaucoup de, un peu de, trop de, assez de, combien de. Beaucoup des is wrong. The one exception is the slightly literary bien des.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I don't eat bread.
questions.why: ne and pas wrap the verb, and the partitive du drops to de inside the negative.

questions.q: Build the sentence: there aren't any children.
questions.why: Il y a des enfants becomes il n'y a pas d'enfants: des collapses to de, and de elides before the vowel of enfants.
The partitive du is the default for an unmeasured amount of something uncountable. English says nothing at all here, which is exactly why it gets left out.

questions.q: Say this out loud — the negative form of « j'ai de l'argent ».
questions.why: de l' collapses to de like every other indefinite and partitive after a negative, then elides to d' before the vowel.

questions.q: Name the three families of article, the question each one answers, and their forms.
a: Definite (which one? and also the general category): le, la, l', les. Indefinite (one of several?): un, une, des. Partitive (how much of it?): du, de la, de l', des. After a negative the indefinite and partitive collapse to de or d', but the definite article and anything after être stay as they are; after an expression of quantity you always get bare de.
questions.why: Choosing an article is choosing between those three questions, so naming the question you are answering is faster than memorising sentences.
